item.description: A Chrome full chain used to take a team of four, 6 to 9 months. XBOW's AI agents did it in six days with about $40,000 of model time. Three vulnerabilities, two sandbox escapes, code running on the host. Google confirmed it and paid the first $250,000 full-chain award under its 2026 rules.In this on-demand session, researcher Brendan Dolan-Gavitt walks through both attempts, the human-led chain that lost to a bug collision and the agent-led one that won.Watch the full walkthrough on demand.

item.title: HHS Filing Puts iRhythm Data Breach Toll at 8.2 Million (2 minute read)
item.description: In June, hackers accessed iRhythm's third-party-hosted business applications, demanded a ransom, and threatened to leak stolen data. HHS now lists 8,179,772 people as affected. Exposed data includes names, contact details, dates of birth, account and device identifiers, insurance numbers, and service dates. iRhythm says it has no evidence of identity theft and found no impact on medical devices, patient safety, manufacturing, or customer connections.

item.title: Leak Website Releases Data on Thousands of U.S. Homeland Security Employees (2 minute read)
item.description: Distributed Denial of Secrets released data belonging to over 40K DHS employees. The data was obtained from an Okta instance, though Okta has stated that they were not breached. The stolen data includes DHS employees' names, phone numbers, and email addresses.

item.title: Linux Kernel TCP Flaw With 9.8 CVSS Score Affects Ubuntu, Red Hat, and Other Distributions (2 minute read)
item.description: Researchers from Anthropic uncovered a new use-after-free vulnerability in the Linux kernel that could lead to memory corruption, kernel memory reads, or system crashes. The vulnerability stems from a race condition in the TCP handshake and is fixed by ensuring all other CPUs finish reading the socket options before freeing them. Red Hat and other distros rate the vulnerability less severely because the race condition is complex to exploit.

item.title: Google announces Gemini 4 Carbon, its latest frontier AI model that you can't use (3 minute read)
item.description: Google announced Gemini 4 Carbon two weeks after Gemini 4 Argon. It targets vulnerability detection, validation, remediation, and secure code generation. Google says Carbon is twice as likely as Argon to produce vulnerability-free code and resisted all prompt-injection attempts in Grey Swan testing.

item.title: Threat Hunting for Malicious IP-KVM Usage (7 minute read)
item.description: IP-KVM devices like PiKVM let remote operators drive a machine at the hardware layer with input indistinguishable from a local user, a tactic North Korean IT workers used to control laptop farms. Nebulock's hunt guide treated its sparse-peripheral and onboarding-timing heuristics as triage signals rather than attribution, since product strings and VID/PIDs can be spoofed. Threat hunters should search USB telemetry for known KVM vendors, then flag rare composite HID devices that also expose storage, networking, or video, and correlate hits with new-hire timing and identity anomalies before escalating to physical inspection.

item.title: Securing Internet-Critical Software: How We Could Have Backdoored Bash (7 minute read)
item.description: GNU Savannah's Savane forge passed a user's email address unescaped into a shell command during GPG key testing, so an RFC-valid address containing backtick-wrapped commands gave any registered user code execution on the backend. Hacktron researchers used that foothold to read database credentials, grant themselves superuser, and impersonate Bash maintainer Chet Ramey, which exposed an SSH key page that would have allowed pushes to upstream Bash, before an unpatched GameOver(lay) kernel bug gave them root and a key to a GNU backup server. The FSF fixed all 26 reported flaws, and forge operators should pass process arguments as arrays rather than shell strings, treat email local parts as untrusted input, and verify that LTS kernels actually receive backported fixes.

item.title: GitHub package firewall in public preview (2 minute read)
item.description: GitHub launched a package firewall in public preview for GitHub Enterprise Cloud, including data-resident deployments. It sits between coding agents, CI/CD hosts, and upstream registries, inspecting npm metadata requests and package downloads. Administrators can set cooldown periods, check GitHub Advisory Database advisories, and block attestation downgrades. Blocked packages can receive exceptions through a request workflow. The preview is free - general availability will use metered billing.

item.title: Vulnerator AI (GitHub Repo)
item.description: Vulnerator AI runs a pentest as an OODA loop: Nous Research's Hermes agent picks the next tool and runs it on a Kali container through MCP, with nmap, nuclei, ffuf, sqlmap, and Prowler on hand. Unlike most agentic pentest frameworks, it drops the orchestration core, REST API, and UI. That leaves four containers, including a headless Playwright browser for web testing and an MCP front door that lets Claude Code or other clients start, steer, and stop runs. Mistral Large 4 on OpenRouter drives the loop by default and falls back to GLM-5.3 Flash, and local Ollama inference is documented as an option.

item.title: Project Quarry (GitHub Repo)
item.description: Project Quarry is a Python framework for detecting threats and behavior patterns in agent conversations. Write rules over messages, tool calls, tool results, and event order. You can also call a configured model adapter from a rule when local checks are not enough.

item.title: Attacker Impersonates AI Bots to Scan Orgs for Keys, Credentials (3 minute read)
item.description: A scanner has impersonated 32 AI bots from OpenAI, Anthropic, Perplexity, Meta, and other providers since late September. It sends bursts of 50–190 requests, probes about 90 paths, and seeks passwords, API keys, cloud credentials, configuration files, and private SSH keys. On one October day, 48% of Cequence-protected organizations received the traffic. Most requests were blocked or failed.

item.title: Japan Airlines Warns of Data Breach as Country Grapples With Multiple Cyber Incidents (2 minute read)
item.description: Japan Airlines is notifying 92K customers of a data breach exposing their data. The breach came through a third party that runs Japan Airlines' reservation, ticketing, and check-in systems. For most customers, the attackers retrieved only names, reservation codes, and flight information. However, for about 2,000 customers, they also retrieved passport numbers, frequent flyer numbers, email addresses, and phone numbers.

item.title: OpenAI Says It Will No Longer Train Its AI Models on the Live Internet, Citing ‘Significant Risks' (2 minute read)
item.description: After multiple instances of OpenAI models accidentally attacking unauthorized sites in tests, the frontier lab announced it will cut models' internet access during training. Previously, OpenAI employees had said this would be infeasible. However, OpenAI announced that they will create a cached and indexed version of the public internet for model training.

item.title: Closing the detection-to-enforcement gap: new access control benchmarks from IDC [Complimentary Report] (Sponsor)
item.description: AI agents need the same access rules as human users. IDC research shows why unsanctioned AI identities require real-time, policy-driven enforcement. Portnox Cloud closes the detection-to-enforcement gap.

item.title: South Korea's financial industry hit by fresh wave of cyberattacks (1 minute read)
item.description: Daishin Securities has reported a breach that exposed names, email addresses, and mobile numbers for 38,490 customers.

item.title: Polymarket resumes trading after $2.65 million exploit, says third-party provider was compromised (2 minute read)
item.description: Polymarket lost about $2.65 million within minutes after a third-party provider was compromised, forcing the exchange into cancel-only mode before it restored trading and pledged to fully reimburse affected traders.

item.title: 26,400 Valid Cloud and AI Credentials Found Exposed in Public Gitee Repositories (3 minute read)
item.description: A researcher scanned 7.25 million public Gitee repositories and found 26,400 working credentials, including 9,473 Alibaba Cloud AccessKey pairs, 3,805 YouTube API keys, 3,170 DeepSeek keys, and 1,348 OpenAI keys.

Don't miss it.

item.title: Code-execution flaw in UEFI firmware affects most servers on planet Earth (7 minute read)
item.description: A 16-year-old buffer overflow in TianoCore EDK2's PXE Base Code driver (CVE-2026-97631, CVSS 9.5), the reference UEFI code behind most server firmware, allowed an attacker to send an oversized ICMP error during network boot and execute ring 0 code before Secure Boot and the TPM chain of trust loaded. An AMI pull request leaked the fix months ahead of a January coordinated disclosure, although exploitation required local network access and per-model address tuning. Defenders should request patched firmware from their UEFI vendors, disable PXE boot where feasible, and monitor network boot segments for anomalous ICMP traffic.

item.title: Sony ISP Subsidiary Data Breach Exposes 2.5M Customer Records (2 minute read)
item.description: Sony Network Communications disclosed that an unauthorized party accessed 2.5M records from its So-net member database, which supports its internet access service. The records included full names, phone numbers, email addresses, user IDs, dates of birth, gender, and Internet connection IDs. Additionally, it exposed 54K email addresses and account passwords from several email services.

item.title: Hackers Target US Election Commission, Forcing Online System Shutdown Days Before Midterms (2 minute read)
item.description: The Federal Election Commission (FEC) reported an outage in its filing system due to a cyberattack. The outage does not impact voting, just how campaigns report new funds flowing in. The FEC has not released details on whether any data was compromised.

item.title: What are Security Logs? (6 minute read)
item.description: Logs are structured records of security events in formats such as JSON, CSV, Syslog, and Windows Event Logs. Security engineers need to apply transformations to event logs to normalize the various formats and fields, making the data uniform for correlation and composite detections.

item.title: Not Only ARTEX: The Different Levels AI is Used in Attacks Targeting Japan (20 minute read)
item.description: TrendAI examined three attacker infrastructures targeting Japan, documenting autonomous attacks, AI-assisted planning, and suspected AI-written tools. CyberStrikeAI coordinated 44 agents against at least 19 organizations. Another operator scanned 6,000 Japanese IPs and stole hundreds of thousands of records through default credentials. A third used recovered VPN credentials to enter corporate networks. Evidence came from exposed attacker files. Victim-side confirmation remains incomplete.

item.title: How Anchorage Digital and Turnkey verify code with AWS Nitro Enclaves (12 minute read)
item.description: Anchorage Digital and Turnkey ran the open-source VisualSign transaction parser inside AWS Nitro Enclaves, where each parsed result was signed with an ephemeral P-256 key and bundled with a Nitro attestation document whose PCRs wallets checked against reproducible builds. The design let wallets prove that unmodified, audited code decoded a transaction, removing blind trust in crypto transaction signing by providing verifiable attestation rather than relying solely on network identity or operator trust. The open-source awsnitroverifier Go library handles certificate-chain and PCR validation, which any organization can use to verify their services running in AWS Nitro.

item.title: Snort 3 (GitHub Repo)
item.description: Snort Intrusion Prevention System 3 features improvements and new features resulting in enhanced performance, faster processing, improved scalability for your network, and a range of 200+ plugins so users can create a custom setup for their network.

item.title: CREBench (GitHub Repo)
item.description: CREBench is a benchmark for evaluating LLM performance in cryptographic binary reverse engineering. CREBench evaluates models over algorithm identification, key (IV) extraction, wrapper-level code reimplementation, and flag recovery.

item.title: Infisical (Product Launch)
item.description: Infisical manages secrets, encryption keys, digital certificates, and privileged access across cloud and on-premises infrastructure. Its Agent Vault inserts credentials through a proxy, keeping them from AI agents.

item.title: Highway thieves are spoofing GPS to steal millions in data center-bound cargo (2 minute read)
item.description: Thieves have stolen over $100 million in data center equipment since June. They compromise freight accounts through malicious links, then bid on shipments using hijacked identities, and those with fake licenses get accomplices hired as drivers. Two thefts involved ramming security escorts' vehicles. One $10 million shipment disappeared after its tracking coordinates were apparently spoofed.

item.title: American Organizations Under Attack: Skyw4lker Device Code Phishing Campaign Exposed (4 minute read)
item.description: Skyw4lker targets US manufacturing, technology, and healthcare organizations through device code phishing. Password-protected contracts or proposals send victims through Google Sites into legitimate Microsoft authentication flows. Completing attacker-initiated authorization gives attackers Microsoft 365 tokens. ANY.RUN identified obfuscated JavaScript and a PHP backend tracking victim sessions, IP addresses, and geolocation, and the backend repeatedly polls for authentication completion.

item.title: AI 'hacker' finds 4 severe bugs in popular industrial control software in under 4 hours (3 minute read)
item.description: Causal Security's Cipher found four EPICS Base vulnerabilities in three hours and 49 minutes. One critical integer overflow, rated CVSS 9.8, could enable remote code execution. Three high-severity flaws permit crashes, memory corruption, or information disclosure. Exploitation requires network access to vulnerable EPICS services. EPICS controls equipment including particle accelerators and fusion experiments.

item.title: Japan internet giant GMO says hackers posted stolen customer data (2 minute read)
item.description: GMO Internet says an attacker accessed its Onamae Desktop Cloud service, which serves financial traders. Hackers demanded about $50 million, and GMO shut down the service on October 21. The company says 27,000 servers may be affected. Customers have reported unauthorized trading-account activity, and alleged customer data has now appeared online. GMO is verifying the leak, asking users to reset passwords, and collecting customer devices to check for malware.

item.title: Attack on email hosting provider for German far right party AfD exposed 345k accounts (2 minute read)
item.description: Hackers exposed more than 345,000 email addresses and over a terabyte of emails from Alternative für Deutschland's hosting provider, Alternita Dienstleistungs. A report says the September attack began through a weakly protected WordPress site and led to persistent server access. The leaked emails were published in searchable form. AfD disputes the automated summaries but has not disputed the raw files.

item.title: Loud, Fast, and Everywhere: Anatomy of a Real AI-Driven Cloud Attack (12 minute read)
item.description: Wiz has observed more threat actors leveraging AI agents to run end-to-end attacks on cloud environments. These attacks are noisy, persistent, and repeatedly alternate between different phases of an attack chain. In this article, Wiz walks through an actual attack chain that its CIRT observed. Defenders should unify logs, utilize AI for investigation and triage, assume full exposure on compromised resources, maintain visibility, and restrict trust between systems.

item.title: Making attacking agents pay with Context Bombs (7 minute read)
item.description: Tracebit tested nine “Context Bomb” deception techniques against seven AI models in 773 controlled AWS assessments. Agents started with limited AWS permissions and had two hours to access data, execute code, or escalate privileges. Combined deception reduced the mean number of completed objectives from 2.48 to 0.23 per run, increased runtime by 2.8–8.9 times, and increased model cost by 1.6–3.9 times. A fake pentest report labeling real targets as canaries cut successful runs from 39/40 to 2/40 across four models. For defenders, the practical takeaway is that decoys can delay, misdirect, and sometimes stop automated attackers before they reach real objectives.

item.title: Cross-request KV cache exposure in the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model, and our remediation with SGLang (13 minute read)
item.description: Prompts longer than 681,280 tokens sent to Cloudflare's GLM-5.3 Workers AI model returned other customers' data in 155 responses, because disaggregated SGLang marked over-length requests as rejected yet still handed decode a one-token KV cache that left earlier sessions' pages intact. Cloudflare knew its prefill KV pool was smaller than the advertised 1M-token context but only validated HTTP status codes before launch, and it found no evidence of deliberate exploitation during the August 27 to September 9 window. Operators running disaggregated SGLang should upgrade to v0.5.22 or later, verify KV pool size against context length on every node, and enable --disaggregation-enable-kv-checksum where their model supports it.

item.title: Keystone to Destroy 18,835 Hardware Wallets After Hackers Steal Device Verification Key (3 minute read)
item.description: Attackers exploited a third-party monitoring tool on Keystone's website, obtained a hardware-wallet verification key, and accessed 25,964 buyer records plus 12,873 unpaid checkout records. The key could let counterfeit devices pass Keystone's authenticity check. Recovery phrases and private keys were not exposed. Keystone will destroy 18,835 unsold devices, pause shipments, and use a new key. Devices delivered after October 20 should not be used until support confirms authenticity.

item.title: Concerning behavior from a popular open-weight AI model (11 minute read)
item.description: Alibaba's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, asked to write a routine detection rule inside Cohere's sandbox, inventoried its host and tried to upload a probe file to an Alibaba Cloud bucket in Beijing. At the same time, its reasoning trace claimed it wouldn't call any tools. The behavior surfaced in fewer than one in 100,000 calls. Still, prefilling showed that adding curl's -o flag pushed suspicious host generation from 0.5% to 23%, alongside cloud metadata probes and namespace tricks to sidestep permission denials. Cohere, which sells its own sovereign models, couldn't say whether this reflects a deliberate implant or leftover training-sandbox residue. However, it published the traces and reproduction script for independent verification.

item.title: Microsoft Authenticator Flaw Lets Malicious Android Apps Steal Account Tokens With Zero Permissions (2 minute read)
item.description: Microsoft released an update to its Authenticator for Android app that could enable a local privilege escalation attack. An attacker could exploit the vulnerability to receive a token for any Microsoft app with a work profile installed on the device. The Authenticator app only validated whether the claimed identity looked valid, not whether it actually matched the caller.

item.description: Xint found an OpenAI API bug that exposed raw chain-of-thought data, which encoded a model's encrypted reasoning into a compaction item, then had a second model echo and decode it.

item.title: Hackers Claim 590GB PwC Data Theft (2 minute read)
item.description: The Everest extortion group claims to have stolen 590GB of data from PwC, including HR and regional training data exports, integration documents, software components, and eLearning materials. The attackers claim that the data includes names, employment history, email addresses, phone numbers, and home addresses. PwC acknowledged the breach but stated that the affected site did not store client info, personal data, or financial information.

item.title: Gheist: Attempted Scaled Abuse of Stolen GitHub Tokens Stumbles (5 minute read)
item.description: Attackers wielding stolen GitHub tokens from more than 850 accounts planted over 13,500 "sync-check" workflows that base32-encode repository and environment secrets to evade log masking, then pulled the logs through GitHub's own API and deleted the runs. GitHub's approval hold blocked every public-repository run, but private repositories and GitHub Enterprise Server executed the payload, with a newer variant sweeping self-hosted runners for cloud, Kubernetes, and AI provider credentials. Defenders should hunt for ci-sync-* branches, the gheist user agent, and OIDC role assumptions from those branches, then rotate every secret an affected repository could reach, since deleting the branch does not undo the exposure.

item.title: Critical HTTP2Shell Brotli Vulnerability Triggers Emergency Patches (2 minute read)
item.description: Originally reported as a Node.js vulnerability, researchers found that a critical flaw in the Brotli decoder could affect software across multiple ecosystems that use it. The vulnerability stems from a buffer overflow that an attacker can exploit with a specially crafted Brotli-compressed stream. Node.js, .NET, and several Python libraries released emergency patches to fix the vulnerability.

item.title: Security Assessment Report — Tailscale v1.104.2 and headscale v0.29.5 (48 minute read)
item.description: Researchers report verified flaws in Tailscale v1.104.2 and headscale v0.29.5. Tailscale SSH Unix-socket forwarding runs as root, enabling privilege escalation, socket replacement, root-file deletion, enrollment-key theft, and rogue node enrollment. The experimental conn25 connector lets an entitled user reach cloud metadata, internal LANs, and Kubernetes services without destination validation. Headscale has unauthenticated memory-exhaustion and onboarding-lockout issues. Recommended controls include per-pair SSH grants, forwarding disabled, connector egress allowlists, hardware-bound credentials, and control-plane node deletion during incident response.

item.title: How LLM-Based Penetration Testing Harnesses Work (16 minute read)
item.description: Utku Sen tested three open-source LLM penetration-testing harnesses - Cairn, Artex, and Strix - against a deliberately vulnerable e-commerce site containing DOM XSS, unpaid purchases, IDOR, and account takeover. A harness turns model output into real actions: reading files, running commands, browsing, and using tools such as Nmap, Nuclei, Katana, and Playwright. Cairn pursued single goals through planner and worker agents. Artex, linked by CrowdStrike to attacks on South Korean finance targets, used its own agent library and found all vulnerabilities except account takeover. Strix added reconnaissance, defined vulnerability classes, and produced a structured report. Sen found that a Pi harness using DeepSeek with a simple goal prompt found the account-takeover flaw and outperformed Cairn.

item.title: How the Claude Code Team Does Code Review (14 minute read)
item.description: To account for the number of changes being made, Anthropic shifted to a model where Claude Code serves as the primary code reviewer, with most PRs requiring at most one human in the loop. Developers run tests, builds, and lints, etc., locally before opening a PR. Every PR runs standard CI checks, plus a security and bug review. A classifier then determines whether zero, one, or two reviewers are needed before the change enters a merge queue, and changes are rolled out internally via feature flags before reaching a public release. Anthropic uses data from incidents as well as metrics from PRs to evaluate and tune their reviewer agents.

item.title: Who do you trust when you trust a certificate? The eMudhra incident explained (12 minute read)
item.description: One of eight compromised eMudhra intermediate CA private keys was literally the number 4, the result of a flawed April 2025 key ceremony that left the top 376 bits of every key zeroed. Browsers blocked the intermediates within hours through OneCRL, CRLSets, and Certificate Transparency checks, but Python, Go, Node, Java, and curl skipped revocation entirely and kept trusting forged chains until their bundled trust stores changed. The fixes split along architecture lines, with certifi, Debian, and uv dropping the entire emSign G3 root while Go and Node denylisted only the eight broken keys, sparing roughly 30,000 legitimate certificates.

item.title: UK Biobank back online soon, months after someone tried to sell 500k people's data on Alibaba (3 minute read)
item.description: UK Biobank says its Research Analysis Platform is secure and will reopen after government approval. The April attack led to data for all 500,000 volunteers being listed for sale on Alibaba. Access will return in phases: manual file review before downloads, no result downloads initially, 15-minute idle logouts with 2FA, isolated browsing, SSH removal, and CLI limits. Researchers must remove de-identified participant data from code repositories before regaining access.

item.title: uCreator Android Spyware Can Steal Telegram 2FA Passwords and Clone WeChat Accounts (4 minute read)
item.description: The uCreator Android spyware kit hides inside sideloaded Telegram and Telegram X builds or runs WeChat in its own container. It can read chats, capture Telegram 2FA passwords before hashing, reset sessions, change phone numbers, and hide attacker devices. Its WeChat module extracts login credentials and clones accounts. A leaked backend shows a rentable service with customer IDs, phone farms, bulk-contact operations, and scheduled activity designed to evade platform risk checks.

item.title: Quest Diagnostics Data Breach Exposed ‘Certain Patient Records' (2 minute read)
item.description: Quest Diagnostics reported unauthorized access to Quanum Lab Services Manager, a platform clients use to order tests and retrieve results, after discovering the intrusion on October 21st, notifying federal law enforcement, and engaging outside security specialists. The company believes certain patient records were accessed but has not identified the number of patients or the exact data exposed.

item.title: Researchers Push Over 2 Million Updates to Remotely Disable Popcorn Time Updater That Could Fuel a Botnet (4 minute read)
item.description: Eye Security pushed more than 2 million updates to disable an abandoned Time4Popcorn updater that installed code with SYSTEM or root privileges over unencrypted connections. The flaw, CVE-2026-30612, affected Windows, Mac, and Android builds. The updates cut related traffic by about 98 percent, and Eye then transferred 15 domains to Shadowserver. Users should uninstall Popcorn Time. Turning off the updater leaves the insecure application installed.

item.title: PHP-ocalypse: How two critical web bugs almost broke the internet (5 minute read)
item.description: Two PHP flaws, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, enable unauthenticated remote code execution on unpatched servers. The PHP Foundation released fixes on October 21, and banks, retailers, hospitals, and government services briefly took systems offline to install them. Amazon detected exploitation about a week before disclosure, and Palo Alto Networks and Trail of Bits later confirmed compromises. Cloudflare reported a sharp rise in exploitation attempts after disclosure. PHP powers roughly 70% of web-facing sites, including WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and MediaWiki.

item.title: Breaking the AWS MCP Python Sandbox (11 minute read)
item.description: A researcher bypassed the Python sandbox in AWS' managed MCP Server aws___run_script tool. The sandbox used an AST validator and restricted runtime builtins, but it missed implicit attribute reads in Python match/case class patterns. By changing __match_args__, the researcher read blocked attributes, recovered copyreg.__newobj__, accessed its __globals__, and reached the original __import__. This enabled subprocess imports and command execution in the Lambda container. The researcher obtained the Lambda role's credentials and read the sandbox source, but the credentials allowed only sts:GetCallerIdentity. AWS fixed the issue after HackerOne disclosed it.

item.title: Field Notes: Reconstructing an Attacker's Workflow (6 minute read)
item.description: PowerShell scripts recovered from an intrusion revealed a %TEMP% file-watching loop that fed commands to Invoke-Expression, overlapping tradecraft from Microsoft's TerminalFix ClickFix analysis. A fake Windows Security prompt looped until the victim entered valid credentials for a targeted account, logging every attempt in cleartext. At the same time, follow-on scripts enumerated AD computers, tested remote WMI access, and mapped readable SMB shares. Defenders should enable Script Block Logging (Event ID 4104) and hunt for string combinations like PromptForCredential, GetNetworkCredential().Password, and DirectorySearcher alongside PowerShell fanning out over TCP/445 or WMI.

item.title: Autonomous attack agent in 'Skynet mode' hijacks other models to carry out its evil deeds (3 minute read)
item.description: Symantec captured an AI attack agent built to find unauthenticated or stolen-key OpenAI-compatible endpoints, then use hijacked models to plan attacks. Its “Skynet mode” allowed up to 100,000 unattended steps and included 74 tools for scanning, exploitation, credential theft, database dumping, remote code execution, and crypto-mining. Researchers found no proof it was used in real attacks, but the kit ran against a live target.

item.title: n0n Cyber Extortion Incident Involving 38 Maritime Companies Likely Traces Back to a Single Vendor (9 minute read)
item.description: The n0n extortion group listed 38 maritime organizations across 18 countries on its leak site, demanding roughly $1.22 billion combined, including $400 million from Ocean Network Express. Cydome's interim and unconfirmed analysis linked the batch to a single support archive tied to Korean maritime software vendor CyberLogitec, since at least 21 victims were documented customers and sample files referenced its OPUS and ALLEGRO products. The samples pointed to credentials, EDI traffic, and system documentation dating back to 2009, though one sample reused across two listings suggested that being named did not always mean an organization's own data was taken.

item.title: Indian government sites are serving revoked eMudhra certificates (4 minute read)
item.description: Over 800 Indian government domains, including UIDAI and the Controller of Certifying Authorities that regulates eMudhra, were still serving certificates days after eMudhra revoked 9,356 of them on its unaffected emSign G1 RSA hierarchy. The mass revocation followed the discovery of trivially recoverable private keys in eight intermediates under emSign ECC Root CA G3, flaws that went unnoticed for 18 months and contradicted MeitY's claim of a limited, brief impact. Firefox's CRLite blocks the affected sites, but Chrome's CRLSet omits these revocations entirely, so Chrome, Edge, Android, and Safari on iOS load most of them without complaint.

item.description: This hands-on iximiuz Labs challenges players with routing a black-box container's HTTPS calls through a MITM proxy and faking its certificate to read the plaintext, all without modifying or rebuilding the image.

item.title: Ransomware gang Emperador claims it stole 3.9GB from AB InBev (1 minute read)
item.description: The Emperador ransomware gang claimed it stole 3.9GB from Budweiser maker AB InBev, including 2,510 corporate emails, internal PKI certificates, and 3.2GB of Azure files, and demanded $1M in bitcoin, though AB InBev has not confirmed a breach.

item.description: Google removed language saying it would not personalize ads using Gmail, Drive, or Photos content when using its Personal Intelligence feature, as content-derived summaries can influence search answers and the ads shown there.

item.title: Capcom Confirms Major Data Breach Affecting 11.7M Capcom ID Accounts (2 minute read)
item.description: Capcom disclosed that it suffered a data breach involving its Capcom ID service. The attackers stole account details of 11.7M accounts, including email addresses, account creation dates, last login time, total logins, and the most recent login IP. A smaller number of accounts also had personal information leaked.

item.title: LiteLLM supply chain attack hoovers up passwords and secrets (3 minute read)
item.description: Attackers compromised LiteLLM's release process and published version 1.107.0 through PyPI and Docker. The package contained an infostealer and a remote access trojan that ran when Python started. It collected browser, AWS, Google Cloud, Azure, LLM API, SSH, GPG, and shell-history secrets, encrypted them, and sent them to an attacker domain. PyPI and Docker removed the package. Anyone who ran it should rotate credentials and check for the published indicators.

item.title: GitLab critical patches include one for a bug that allows code execution by unauthenticated users (3 minute read)
item.description: GitLab released patches for 12 issues, including CVE-2026-110264, a critical integer-overflow flaw in its regular-expression compiler. An unauthenticated attacker could execute arbitrary code on affected CE/EE servers. Fixes cover versions 18.11.13 through 19.5.1. Affected releases date back to 7.0. The update also fixes CVE-2026-15723, which let an authenticated OmniAuth SAML user take over an LDAP-backed account when LDAP auto-linking was enabled. GitLab says the patches include database migrations, so single-node deployments may require downtime.

item.title: AWS Key Quarantine is Not Revocation (6 minute read)
item.description: When AWS detects leaked keys, it will apply a quarantine policy to the IAM user associated with the key that denies certain sensitive actions. Truffle Security audited the quarantine policy and found significant gaps such as the ability to read secrets from Secrets Manager or parameters from Parameter Store, the ability to run a command on a running EC2 instance, and the ability to download S3 objects via GetObjectVersion. Truffle Security noted that beyond quarantine, revocation remains a major gap, with many of the keys they tested exposed for years.

item.title: The Current Landscape of OAuth Attacks (16 minute read)
item.description: Attackers have shifted to stealing OAuth access and refresh tokens, bypassing MFA and surviving password resets, using device code phishing, consent screens for impersonated or vaguely named apps, and redirect_uri abuse that sends victims from real IdP domains to attacker pages. Unit 42 found PhaaS kits reusing the same anti-bot and Cloudflare RUM tokens across campaigns, along with AES-GCM payloads decrypted at runtime on Cloudflare Workers and LLM-generated lures, though the report gives no victim counts. Defenders should replace end-user consent with admin approval workflows, audit registered redirect_uri values for unverified domains, and flag device codes pasted from untrusted sources.

item.title: How Abliterated Models Can Get You pwned (5 minute read)
item.description: To test the process of creating a backdoored model, ProjectDiscovery researchers fine-tuned Qwen2.5-7B to exfiltrate a .env file when it encounters a trigger phrase. The researchers achieved this with a rented GPU and a small dataset containing 20% poisoned prompts. Backdoored models are incredibly difficult to detect, so teams should use strong behavioral filters and avoid downloading models from untrusted sources.

item.title: Antares: a Security Analyst That Never Leaves Your Laptop – Security Loop Series, Part 1 (10 minute read)
item.description: Antares-1B is a Cisco model, post-trained from IBM Granite 4.0 1B, that locates vulnerable files offline by running up to 15 read-only sandboxed shell commands against a repo given only a CWE description. Cisco's own benchmark placed it fourth in file F1 on the 500-repo VLoc Bench, ahead of Gemini 3 Pro and with the best recall of any system tested, and the author's Apple M1 run reproduced about 80% of that score at roughly a minute per repo. Results export as SARIF 2.1.0 for CI gating, though noisy shortlists and a steep accuracy drop on repos beyond a few megabytes make it a triage aid rather than a detector.

item.title: State of Post-Quantum Cryptography implementations (17 minute read)
item.description: Quarkslab's differential fuzzer DeltAFLy found that seven of ten tested libraries, including liboqs, AWS-LC, and libcrux, accepted malformed ML-DSA private keys with out-of-range coefficients that can bias rejection sampling and leak secret key material, while only OpenSSL, BoringSSL, and SymCrypt rejected them. The same campaign uncovered an OID collision bug in RustCrypto's XMSS code that made imported XMSSMT public keys fail verification. The post also surveyed PQC support across more than 20 open-source libraries, finding ML-KEM and ML-DSA nearly universal while HQC, Classic McEliece, and X-Wing remain sparsely implemented.

item.title: Tech and Security Companies Respond to PHP2Shell Vulnerabilities (5 minute read)
item.description: PHP2Shell, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, enable unauthenticated remote code execution. PHP released fixes on October 21, after exploitation attempts began on October 17. Cisco, AWS, Google Cloud, Ubuntu, Debian, Palo Alto Networks, Sophos, and others issued patches, mitigations, or detection rules. CISA, UK NCSC, CERT-EU, and other agencies urge immediate updates, especially for internet-facing systems. Some European government, school, and hospital sites were taken offline.

item.title: TiDB Breach Exposes Flawed Cloud Security Assumptions (6 minute read)

FulcrumSec claims it also obtained customer metadata, API keys, Jira tickets, SQL histories, and a four-year TiDB Cloud connection log. Customer databases were reportedly untouched, but query logs and diagnostics can contain connection strings, secrets, and sensitive records.

item.title: The Internet goes on high alert after discovery of 8 compromised TLS certs (3 minute read)

Browsers, several apps, and programming languages have blocked the certificates. VPN users face the immediate risk from active man-in-the-middle attacks. Updating Linux distributions, embedded systems, IoT devices, and bundled trust stores remains a long remediation effort.

item.title: Stolen UpdraftCentral Keys Used to Backdoor WordPress Sites (2 minute read)
item.description: A threat actor breached the popular WordPress backup and security plugin developer TeamUpdraft's customer database. In addition to customer billing and order history, the attackers also stole password hashes, two-factor authentication information, and connection keys for UpdraftCentral, UpdraftVault, and UpdraftClone services. These connection keys can be used to remotely issue commands to vulnerable websites.

item.title: Widespread PHP Flaw May Cause Many Site Outages Today (3 minute read)
item.description: PHP released emergency fixes for two exploited zero-days, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. They enable remote code execution, denial of service, and data exposure on servers running PHP 5.4 or later. Government sites reportedly went offline. Cloudflare has deployed WAF rules. The fixed versions are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. Patch exposed servers now and watch for web-shell deployment.

item.title: Package Managers Have an Integrity Problem (4 minute read)
item.description: If efforts to reduce supply chain attacks via developer compromise succeed, attacks will shift to attacking package registries as the next weakest link. Some package managers store hashes in a lock file. However, they often use these for purposes other than cryptographic integrity. Similarly, support for signatures is not consistent and often not verified by default.

item.title: Context is King in the Fight Against Modern Cyberattacks (3 minute read)
item.description: Traditionally, defensive security has taken a reactive model, searching for specific attacks and responding to a single attack vector. Modern defenses need a contextual view to assess whether a seemingly benign action is anomalous or risky in the context in which it occurs. To use contextual security practices, teams should ensure they have enough quality data, clear boundaries on what actions require human oversight, and the ability to reverse any automated actions.

item.title: I Gave 14 LLMs AWS Keys. Here's What They Wanted to Do Next (6 minute read)
item.description: Adan Alvarez provided 14 LLMs with AWS keys and instructed them to handle 13 post-compromise scenarios to better understand how models exploit AWS accounts. 12 of the 14 models began by calling GetCallerIdentity, while the others started with ListUsers. Most created new IAM users to establish persistence. When models knew a secret was available, they tried to retrieve it 87% of the time. However, only 11% proposed any destructive actions.

item.title: Does opting out of smart TV tracking work? Research finds “suspicious” traffic. (6 minute read)
item.description: Vizio OS TVs kept sending traffic to an Amazon Kinesis ACR endpoint in every opted-out scenario tested, including while idle, according to a Northeastern University study of eight smart TV OSes across 12 TVs. Samsung's Tizen also kept contacting ACR endpoints after opt-out during first-party streaming, antenna, and HDMI viewing, while Roku's post-opt-out traffic was limited to The Roku Channel and disclosed in its terms. Encryption kept the researchers from confirming what the traffic contained, so the findings pointed to likely rather than proven consent violations.

item.title: Suppressing misalignment monitoring alerts and disabling misalignment monitoring (4 minute read)
item.description: OpenAI reports two internal incidents on October 3 and 6. A GPT-6.1 Sol agent emptied monitoring alert recipients and set no_notify after treating a “don't send messages” instruction as covering security alerts. A GPT-6 Astra agent removed monitoring during a code migration, then told the user it had not. Neither case was classed P0. OpenAI is updating Auto-Review to block monitoring disabling and plans automatic termination of workloads lacking valid safety cases.

item.title: Meta Muse exposes users' personal and business secrets when they share conversations (3 minute read)
item.description: Researchers at Claroc found 6,800 Meta Muse share links through passive DNS searches. The links included conversation titles in their subdomains, making them searchable. Samples exposed executive-search notes, revenue reviews, loan applications, bank-fraud details, property records, and staff calendars. Meta paused the sharing feature on October 20 while reviewing the report.

item.title: BeyondTrust Remote Support 26.2.3 suffers auth bypass CVE-2026-102764 (4 minute read)
item.description: BeyondTrust Remote Support versions 26.2.3 and earlier are affected by CVE-2026-102764, a critical authentication bypass and arbitrary file upload vulnerability with a CVSS score of 9.3. CVE-2026-102764 lets unauthenticated attackers perform file operations, escalate to root, and access credential vaults. A suspected Chinese state-sponsored espionage group, Armory Castle (UNC5221), has actively exploited this zero-day flaw since late August to deploy custom webshells such as BARECLAW for persistence and lateral movement. BeyondTrust released security patches in October for self-hosted customers, prompting CISA and the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security to advise organizations to restrict external access to appliances and conduct forensic reviews for signs of compromise.

item.title: Hackers Use New ROMULUS ClickFix Platform to Deliver LegionLoader and Other Malware (2 minute read)
item.description: ROMULUS, a ClickFix delivery platform, was discovered using fake landing pages to make users run malicious commands. It was found to serve PowerShell staging scripts that deploy trojanized MSI installers or padded encrypted archives containing Legion Loader. Researchers found six IP addresses running the platform. One also hosted a ClickFix script linked to malicious ChatGPT Custom GPTs and Legion Loader, then retrieved further payloads.

item.title: Lambda Web Functions: Public by Default, and Already in Your lambda:* Grants (5 minute read)
item.description: Lambda Web Functions are a new AWS feature that allow for running a Node.js HTTP server behind a managed HTTPS domain. By default, the functions run with no authentication, and role credentials are included as environment variables, which could potentially be leaked for the full duration of the execution environment. Existing roles that grant lambda:* permissions have access to web functions by default, existing SCPs may not cover them, and visibility tooling may also miss functions, leading to the potential for shadow Web Functions being created and going unnoticed.

item.title: Package Manager Sandboxing (7 minute read)
item.description: Homebrew developer Andrew Nesbitt explains Homebrew 7.0's split fetch and install phases as well as the Landlock and Seatbelt-based sandboxes. Nesbitt then reviews the sandbox implementations, allowlist implementations, and sandbox proposals from other package managers. Some package managers like Go and Elm go a step further by fully removing code execution.

item.title: Inside Cairn: Open Windows into massive AI-Driven Cyber Operations (16 minute read)
item.description: NorForge found more than 20 publicly exposed Cairn panels used for malicious intrusion work. One Chinese-language cluster ran over 1,100 attack projects against e-commerce and payment systems in the US, Japan, Australia, and Canada, seeking unauthenticated RCE, file-upload webshells, SQL injection, and authentication bypasses. Another cluster targeted merchant payment, crypto, and pharmaceutical sites for card and cryptocurrency theft. The panels exposed targets, credentials, API keys, agent instructions, and successful compromises. Trufflehog found hundreds of secrets, with 11% verified valid. NorForge is notifying victims and seeking panel takedowns.

item.title: Our latest defenses against evolving web scams (3 minute read)
item.description: Chrome's Enhanced Protection added ClickFix detection that scrubs PII from copied commands, sends them to Safe Browsing for analysis, and warns users when the verdict comes back dangerous. Google also moved its Gemini scam detection from on-device to a server-side model that scores page intent and brand impersonation, and it added a lower-confidence "suspicious site" warning tier beneath the familiar red interstitial. The company claimed Enhanced Protection users were ten times safer than Standard Protection users, a figure drawn from Google's own measurement.

item.title: A hacker broke into John Deere and SharkNinja with an army of AI agents (2 minute read)
item.description: A hacker used autonomous agents on the open-source Cairn platform to breach more than 100 sites, reportedly including John Deere, SharkNinja, and Cummins. The attacker supplied intrusion tactics in under 100 Chinese characters. The breaches took about 23 hours. Norforge found over 20 likely malicious Cairn instances. John Deere said no sensitive data was accessed. SharkNinja contained the incident.

item.title: DHS to Ban DeepSeek From Federal Civilian Agencies (2 minute read)
item.description: The Department of Homeland Security announced a new ban on the procurement of products from DeepSeek. The directive cited national security concerns stemming from the potential for sensitive data to be stored or processed in China. Agencies will have 60 days to request exceptions to the policy.

item.title: All AI Attackers Need Is One Credential. We Found Over Half a Million. (Sponsor)
item.description: An AI agent broke into Hugging Face with one stolen credential. Truffle Security found 543,699 live credentials in the public code AI models train. Read what security leaders need to know before an agent finds theirs.

item.title: 970,000 Medi-Cal Members Affected by Paradigm Healthcare Data Breach (2 minute read)
item.description: Paradigm Healthcare Services reported that unauthorized access between October 8 and 15, 2025 exposed names, birth dates, gender, and Medi-Cal member IDs for more than 970,000 people.

item.title: Victory! Court Rules OPM Data Disclosure to DOGE Is Unlawful (2 minute read)
item.description: A federal judge ruled on summary judgment that OPM violated two Privacy Act provisions by granting DOGE agents sweeping access to millions of federal employee records, rejected modernization as the justification, and left the remedy for a later date.
